rationale: The incumbent is over budget in the article and in several assessment fields, so this edition retells the article well within its ceiling and returns a complete assessment. The judgment is restated, not changed. The case stays unresolved, the Great Pyramid claim contradicted, the Pumapunku claim weakly supported, and every other carried verdict stands, with three exceptions. Each applies the rule for claims held on a source statement alone, which the incumbent's assessment predates. GEO-C502 (Engelbach's experimental basis) moves from weakly_supported to unresolved: it has no admitted evidence, and GEO-E002, on sibling claims, itself calls the characterisation unverified. GEO-C913 (PP1 picked from loose debris) and GEO-C918 (interior subsample PP1C) move from well_supported to provisionally_supported. Neither has evidence of its own, so each rests on a disclosed basis: GEO-E057 and GEO-E058 respectively, both attached to the parent GEO-C004. Selection adds two claims so that every account in the accounts field has a graded claim. GEO-C511 carries Fóti's reading of the Aswan pounders and is graded contradicted, low confidence, on GEO-E045. GEO-C580 carries the Andean plant-acid and guano chemistry and is graded unresolved on GEO-E059 and GEO-E064. The prose already discussed both without linking them. Header answers now lead with the answer: the live dispute is Pumapunku, and the settling test is an independent comparison against natural Khapia andesite. Component labels and notes are in plain words, without ids. The salt, Egypt and Pumapunku sections keep their decisive observations and drop repetition. The Stonehenge match is shortened and the radiocarbon aside dropped as less decisive. All five plates are kept. The article groups Davidovits' pyramid and Pumapunku variants under one account; the accounts field lists them separately and is kept unchanged. No research item has been settled since the incumbent: al-Suyūṭī has been read but the other Arabic authors have not, so GEO-R001 stays open. The crux order is kept. This candidate also corrects three malformed claim-link markers in the previous attempt.
article:
Were some of the world's great stone monuments poured rather than carved — mixed from crushed or gathered rock and a mineral binder, and set in place like concrete? The idea has been tested properly in one place and hardly at all in another. At the Great Pyramid, every independent microscope study reads the stone as natural limestone. The one study that also examined a genuine artificial stone found none of its signatures in the monument. There, [the claim that some blocks are cast]{claim=GEO-C020} is contradicted. At Pumapunku in Bolivia, one team reports organic matter inside the andesite that it says natural rock should not hold, and nobody else has looked. So whether [at least one great monument contains cast stone]{claim=GEO-C022} remains open — and most of the tests that would close it are cheap.

{plate:IMG-GEO-P01}

At Aswan, beside the largest abandoned obelisk in Egypt, visitors are invited to strike a granite block with one of the rounded dolerite stones ancient workers are thought to have used. According to the proponent literature, [no visitor has ever reproduced one of the smooth scooped depressions that line the quarry walls]{claim=GEO-C002}. Nobody has counted the attempts or examined the block, so the anecdote proves little. But it points at the real question. Nobody serious doubts that Egyptians built the pyramids and Andeans built Tiwanaku. The question is how the hardest stone was worked — and whether some of it was made instead. Casting needs no lost civilisation, only forgotten chemistry, which is why it can be tested.

## Four accounts

In the orthodox account, stone was quarried, carved with stone and copper tools and fire, hauled and dressed in place. The French chemist Joseph Davidovits proposes two instances. Pyramid casing and backing blocks are limestone re-bound in an alkali 'geopolymer' cement. Pumapunku's andesite was cast from natural volcanic sand with a binder of plant acids and seabird guano. A revision by Barsoum and colleagues at Drexel University makes the pyramid binder a lime-and-silica cement, the chemistry of a mortar. And the researcher Marcell Fóti proposes a natron route: stone etched or bound with waterglass made from natron and heat, with the Aswan pounders and shafts serving as processing tools. Each account predicts something different inside the stone.

## The case for carving

The orthodox account is strong. Unfinished monuments still lie attached to bedrock; the Aswan obelisk was abandoned when its granite cracked. Tools survive in quantity. Geochemistry matches monument stone to quarries: at Stonehenge, fifty of fifty-two sarsens share one chemical profile, and one of them matches the West Woods area about 25 km away. The account's gaps are quantitative. In a few places it needs more time, more hands or better technique than anyone has yet shown, and those places are where this case lives.

## Aswan: rates and tools

The pounding account of granite quarrying is commonly traced to Reginald Engelbach's 1922 report on the obelisk. Fóti's book says [its experimental basis was one self-conducted hour of hand-pounding, with no mass measured and a workforce read off groove spacing]{claim=GEO-C502}. This site has not checked that description against Engelbach's text, and the same book misstates three other sources, so it stands as Fóti's report. The modern number is firmer: [photogrammetry of a dolerite pounder on granite measured about 216 cubic centimetres an hour at 85 strikes a minute]{claim=GEO-C001}. Its authors say that rate tells against pounders as the only method.

That strains the orthodox timeline without favouring moulds: fire-setting, chisels or more labour would absorb the shortfall. Nor are the pounders strange. A survey by Egyptian antiquities inspectors and a Norwegian geologist traces the dolerite to dykes in the local granite. It also finds tool quarries near the obelisk, with pounder-sized blanks beside them. That weighs against [Fóti's reading that the pounders were brought in to grind or tamp a casting mix]{claim=GEO-C511}, though nobody has studied what their wear was made on. Then there are [shafts some five metres deep beside the trench, said to be too narrow to swing a pounder at the bottom]{claim=GEO-C006}. They are test pits to one side and settling vessels to the other, and nobody without a stake in the answer has measured them.

## Ingredients and pictures

The natron route starts from a fact nobody disputes. Egypt had [industrial-scale natron deposits, the glassmakers' alkaline flux, worked from antiquity and declining sharply in the seventh to ninth centuries AD]{claim=GEO-C011}. Natron, heat and silica make waterglass, and [the roughly 850 °C needed was within reach of charcoal and bellows]{claim=GEO-C010}. The only support here is a proponent's appeal to early glassmaking, though ancient metallurgy makes it easy to believe. But the natron studies concern glass, not stone, and heat in a crucible is not industrial processing. The proposed discovery story, that [long-used fire pits accidentally make stone from ash]{claim=GEO-C013}, rests on one unattributed anecdote.

The firmest point is feasibility: [limestone can be re-formed into large, hard, natural-looking blocks with ancient materials]{claim=GEO-C012}. Davidovits' institute reports multi-ton demonstration blocks, never independently analysed. Separately, lime and diatomaceous earth form a calcium-silicate cement at room temperature. That feasibility is why the case is a question and not a fantasy. It is not evidence that anyone did it.

{plate:IMG-GEO-P05}

In the Tomb of Rekhmire an 18th-Dynasty mural shows rows of crucibles tended by workers with poles. Egyptology reads it as metal casting; Fóti argues [the scale and apparatus fit mineral or waterglass processing better]{claim=GEO-C005}. Egyptologists have not engaged the argument. It would be settled by asking what residues each reading predicts and looking for them.

## The salt

The proponents' favourite historical detail comes from the ninth century. When Caliph al-Maʾmūn's men broke into the Great Pyramid, [they found the chamber walls coated with salt]{claim=GEO-C003} — a centimetre and a half of it, in the Geopolymer Institute's telling. Salt is odd in dry quarried limestone and expected in stone that set wet with natron.

The principal Arabic accounts were gathered by al-Suyūṭī in the fifteenth century and translated in 1939. They tell the story of the breach twice and in detail: fire and vinegar, a wall twenty cubits thick, a granite basin holding 'nothing but worn out pieces of rope'. They never mention salt. The web page carrying the salt report names no medieval author. It dates the entry to 820, where the translator puts the caliph's arrival in Egypt in 832. Other medieval authors remain unread, and one passage in them would revive the story; the accounts read so far do not contain it.

The modern salt is real. A 2026 conservation study found [the white crust in the Queen's Chamber and a nearby corridor to be halite — common salt — with only calcite and quartz beside it]{claim=GEO-C907}. But the same paper records halite crusts at other Egyptian limestone sites, including the Sphinx, which is carved from Giza bedrock. It also cites geologists who describe [halite as native to the plateau's limestone, laid down from evaporating seawater]{claim=GEO-C906}; this site has not read their book directly. So [the claim that the pyramid carries salt that comparable natural limestone lacks]{claim=GEO-C506} fails; the proponents' comparison was with European cathedrals. Both accounts predict salt in the blocks, so it cannot choose between them. The surface record is also unreliable, because [almost no megalithic site has a complete published restoration history]{claim=GEO-C594}. Inside the pyramid, cleaning and patching in 1995–97 went undocumented, and salt barely visible in 2022 had spread widely two years later. One cheap test remains: does unworked Giza bedrock grow halite?

## Egypt: inside the stone

{plate:IMG-GEO-P03}

The pyramid claim covers casing, top and backing blocks, not the core. Two laboratory results favour it. In 2006 the Drexel group reported phases combining silicon, calcium and magnesium 'in ratios that do not exist in any of the potential limestone sources'. It conceded that nature 'could have — however unlikely' produced them. In 2011 an overlapping team used nuclear magnetic resonance to read a casing stone from the Bent Pyramid, an earlier pyramid at Dahshur. It found Tura limestone grains in a calcium-silicate gel 'formed by human intervention'.

Against them stand four examinations under the petrographic microscope, the geologist's basic tool, all finding natural limestone. Folk and Campbell saw bedding, burrows, fragile worm tubes and fractures confined to single blocks — things geology makes and moulds do not. Harrell and Penrod found the proponents' showcase 'Lauer sample' to be local limestone with no zeolite cement. Freestone and Middleton examined a British Museum casing fragment. The cristobalite once called synthetic proved to be an ordinary sedimentary mineral. And Jana examined casing stones beside natural Tura limestone and a genuine Davidovits-made geopolymer. That artificial stone was a positive control: it shows what a binder's signature looks like when it is really there. The 2006 silicon-rich spheres turned up in the natural stone too. The geopolymer's binder, rich in sodium, potassium and aluminium, appeared in no casing stone.

On that record the pyramid claim is contradicted. Two objections remain. Davidovits disputes that his critics had the authentic Lauer sample, and Egypt's antiquities authority says the 2006 samples were taken without permission. And Jana's negative applies to the alkali recipe. Nobody has looked for the 2011 calcium-silicate cement, which at a few per cent might hide from bulk chemistry. That is an objection to the verdict, not evidence for casting.

## Pumapunku: the open question

{plate:IMG-GEO-P04}

Here is the only laboratory evidence from a disputed monument that reads as artificial. Two 2019 papers by the Davidovits group [report organic matter and microstructures in Pumapunku stone that the authors argue natural rock should not contain]{claim=GEO-C004}. On that basis [some andesite and red sandstone blocks there are held to be geopolymer-cast]{claim=GEO-C021}. No independent laboratory has re-examined the stone. That makes the claim weakly supported: the only direct evidence points toward casting, and it comes from one interested team.

What was analysed matters. The sandstone came from a documented slab. The andesite, by the authors' own account, [was picked by its flat surface from loose fragments lying outside the protected monument area]{claim=GEO-C913}, not cut from any identified block. The obvious reply is that organic matter in a stone lying in the open is dirt. Expecting it, the team cut into the fragment and [report the same carbon- and nitrogen-bearing matter in the interior, beneath feldspar crystals]{claim=GEO-C918}. That is the strongest part of the result, because surface dirt alone no longer explains it. But it is the same team and the same fragment, and their instrument reads elements, not molecules.

The authors make three admissions. First, nitrogen could not be measured properly, and they cannot tell leftover guano from binder. That leaves [the proposed chemistry of plant acids and a guano hardener]{claim=GEO-C580} asserted: its reported laboratory replication comes without data and used modern chemicals. Second, they compared the monument andesite with no natural andesite at all. Third, amorphous pockets in Tiwanaku andesite were noted in 1892 by travellers with no stake in the matter. That shows the feature recurs, but not whether it is organic or volcanic glass.

A radiocarbon date on the organic matter was promised in 2019 and has not been found. A date near AD 600 would count for casting; a modern one would point to contamination. At Giza, features read as artificial under the electron microscope turned up in natural stone once someone checked. Nobody has run that check here.

The standing counter-evidence is a 1971 Bolivian study tracing the sandstones to natural quarries. But a quarry match cannot tell dressed stone from stone cast with sand from the same quarry. The proponents' current model is sharper, and so more testable: [the andesite was cast from natural, uncrushed volcanic sand from Cerro Khapia, stockpiled at the lakeshore village of Iwawe, and the abandoned 'tired stones' were never building material]{claim=GEO-C903}. Both sides put the andesite's source at Khapia, so chemistry cannot separate them, but the ground can. The mountain will show either quarry faces and dressing debris, or loose sand and none. The excavators' own description of the Iwawe deposit is a second check.

## Can a quarry match see a binder?

{plate:IMG-GEO-P02}

The casting side's broadest reply to provenance work is that [standard quarry-matching methods cannot see hydrogen, carbon or oxygen, and so cannot tell carved quarry stone from stone cast with aggregate from that quarry]{claim=GEO-C030}. For X-ray fluorescence and mass spectrometry that is correct: crushed rock keeps its metal fingerprint, and a quarry match is not proof of carving. But the reply reaches less far than claimed. It lists X-ray diffraction as blind, yet diffraction reads crystalline phases and is how critics looked for zeolite cement. It lists nuclear magnetic resonance as blind to silicon, which is exactly what the pro-casting 2011 study measured. Above all, it does not touch direct microscopy. Cast stone needs a binder, binders leave signatures, and the Egyptian positive control shows those signatures are visible when present.

## What would change our mind

The strongest case for casting that this record does not answer runs as follows. The negative Egyptian studies were built around the alkali recipe, and the calcium-silicate cement has never been looked for. The one monument whose stone reads as artificial has been examined only by its proponents — who found the organic matter inside the stone, under its crystals.

The strongest case against is equally plain. Every time anyone outside the proponent camp has examined monument stone, it has read as natural, down to fossil worm tubes. The Andean fragment that reads otherwise was picked up off the ground by its looks and never compared with the rock it supposedly differs from.

Toward casting:
- a documented refit of the analysed andesite fragment to a catalogued block, or an independent laboratory finding the same interior matter in a catalogued fragment, tested against natural Khapia andesite;
- a radiocarbon date near AD 600 on that matter;
- a blinded test finding a calcium-silicate cement in securely sourced casing stone that a broad suite of natural limestone lacks;
- a magnetic survey of many pyramid blocks sharing one field-aligned direction, as stone that set in place would and quarried, rotated blocks would not;
- Khapia without quarry faces, and the Iwawe deposit a natural sand store of the building period.

Toward carving:
- the fragment's origin staying undocumented while its features turn up in ordinary Khapia andesite;
- a modern radiocarbon date;
- the sandstone's unusual matrix reproduced in natural regional sandstone;
- a targeted search for the cement in casing stone finding nothing;
- halite growing on unworked Giza bedrock;
- quarry faces on Khapia, with the Iwawe deposit turning out to be chips from shaping blocks.

## Where it stands

The headline claim is existential — at least one monument — so it cannot be settled by averaging. Egypt, tested with methods that can see a binder, came out against. Pumapunku has been examined by one team, on a fragment of uncertain standing. An existential claim is neither refuted by one failed instance nor supported by an untested one, and the decisive test has so far been run at the wrong site. Much of what would close the question is cheap. Ask where the andesite fragment came from, and test one with a catalogue number instead. Read the Iwawe excavation report. Walk Khapia's outcrops. The scoop marks at Aswan, meanwhile, still wait for someone to measure them properly.

assessment.synthesis: The thesis (GEO-C022) is existential, so it is judged by its instances, and it stays unresolved: one instance is contradicted and the other has never been independently tested. Egypt (GEO-C020) is contradicted. GEO-E018, GEO-E019 and GEO-E021 read pyramid stone as natural limestone. GEO-E020's genuine geopolymer control shows an alkali binder is plainly visible when present and absent from casing stone, and that the Si-rich spheres of GEO-E012 occur in natural Tura stone. GEO-E017's calcium-silicate reading is the surviving objection: it lies outside GEO-E020's alkali test, but no record has looked for that binder and found it. The salt no longer supports GEO-C020 (GEO-E033). The medieval report (GEO-C003) is uncited (GEO-E029) and absent from al-Suyūṭī (GEO-E027). The modern halite (GEO-C907, GEO-E030) also effloresces at the carved Sphinx (GEO-E031) and is reported native to Giza limestone (GEO-E032, on GEO-C506). Undocumented 1990s cleaning removes any surface baseline (GEO-C594, GEO-E034). Pumapunku (GEO-C021) is weakly supported. GEO-E006 and GEO-E007 are positive but come from one team, and the andesite was a loose surface find (GEO-E057) with no natural comparator (GEO-E060). The interior occurrence (GEO-E058, on GEO-C004) makes surface dirt an incomplete explanation. The only negative, GEO-E008, is a sandstone provenance study that cannot exclude same-quarry aggregate. The methods critique (GEO-C030) holds for PXRF and ICP-MS (GEO-E024) but not against binder-aware petrography (GEO-E020). The Aswan records bear on pounding, not casting. The evidence record whose removal would most change the case verdict is GEO-E020. Without its positive control, the Egyptian branch would drift toward mixed, GEO-C030 would stand unanswered, and the case would move toward mixed.
assessment.steelman: The negative Egyptian literature tested Davidovits' alkali recipe and then stopped. GEO-E020's control was an alkali geopolymer, and its author concedes a binder near 5 wt% might not register in bulk chemistry. GEO-E017 reads a Bent Pyramid casing stone by solid-state NMR as Tura grains in an amorphous calcium-silicate gel, and has drawn no published rebuttal. GEO-E022 shows lime and diatomaceous earth form such a gel at room temperature. GEO-E012's Si–Ca–Mg ratios, absent from all six nearby candidate quarries, have not been reproduced in natural stone by any record here. At Pumapunku the proponents anticipated the contamination objection and cut into the fragment. GEO-E058 reports the same carbon- and nitrogen-bearing matter beneath plagioclase crystals, which proponents read as excluding surface dirt. The sandstone result (GEO-E006) comes from a documented architectural slab, not loose debris. No independent laboratory has re-examined either stone. The only negative, GEO-E008, predates modern analysis and concerns sandstone provenance, which GEO-C030's narrow point shows cannot see a binder. A proponent can say without error that the answer to the Andean result is absent, not negative.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: At least one major megalithic monument contains man-made cast stone: blocks made by binding processed mineral inputs rather than carved from natural rock. The two instances tested are casing and backing blocks of the Great Pyramid and the andesite and red sandstone of Pumapunku in Bolivia.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: The live dispute is at Pumapunku: whether one team's organic and glassy findings, in a loose andesite fragment and a sandstone slab, would survive independent testing against natural rock. In Egypt every independent study reads the stone as natural. What remains there is whether those tests, built for an alkali recipe, also exclude a lime–silica cement, and whether the disputed samples were the right objects. The pyramid's salt no longer discriminates, because both accounts predict it.
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: An independent laboratory testing a documented Pumapunku andesite fragment against natural Khapia andesite, with criteria fixed in advance, would settle the open branch. Alongside it: establish where the analysed fragment came from, date its organic matter, read the Iwawe excavation report, and survey Cerro Khapia for quarry faces or natural sand. For Egypt: blinded NMR of casing stone against a broad natural limestone suite, and a magnetic survey of many blocks.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: The stone was quarried, carved and hauled with attested means: locally quarried dolerite pounders, copper tools, fire-setting, sledges and large organised crews. Half-cut monuments abandoned in quarries, tool-production quarries, worker settlements and provenance matches such as Stonehenge's Stone 58 to West Woods support this. Pyramid stone shows bedding, fossils and fractures confined to single blocks, which moulds do not make, and a real geopolymer control shows what a binder looks like when present. The pyramid's salt is halite, found also on the carved Sphinx and reported native to Giza limestone. Slow measured pounding rates mean more labour or supplementary methods, not manufacture. At Pumapunku the andesite came from Cerro Khapia as dressed blocks and the sandstone from identified quarries. The amorphous pockets are natural volcanic glass noted in 1892. Organic matter in a loose fragment lying in the open is contamination or infiltration.

components.label: The Great Pyramid's casing and backing blocks
components.note: Four independent microscope studies read the stone as natural, one with a real artificial-stone control. An untested lime–silica cement and a sample-identity dispute remain.

components.label: Pumapunku andesite and sandstone
components.note: The only monument stone that reads as artificial, but from one team, on a loose andesite fragment, with no natural comparison and no independent re-examination.

components.label: Ingredients and feasibility
components.note: Egypt's natron supply is established and artificial limestone can be made; the fire-pit discovery story is one anecdote. Feasibility is not occurrence.

components.label: The pyramid salt
components.note: The salt is real halite, but it also crusts the carved Sphinx and is reported native to Giza limestone. The medieval salt report has no traceable author.

components.label: Can quarry matching see a binder?
components.note: Correct that trace-element matching cannot see a binder; wrong about diffraction and NMR; silent on direct microscopy, which can.

components.label: Aswan quarrying and tools
components.note: One solid measurement strains a pounding-only timeline; the other quarry observations are unmeasured, and the pounders were quarried locally. None of it evidences casting.

researchPriority.reason: The decisive tests are cheap — a records request for the Pumapunku fragment, a desk read, a field walk, a blinded re-analysis — but the tested branch came out contradicted, so a reversal is unlikely.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Existential, so judged by its instances. The Egyptian instance (GEO-C020) is contradicted by binder-aware petrography. The Andean instance (GEO-C021) rests on one team's positive records with no independent negative. GEO-E009, the Stonehenge match attached here, undermines only weakly because a quarry match cannot see a binder (GEO-C030). One contradicted instance and one untested instance is a gap, not a collision of evidence, so the verdict is unresolved rather than contradicted or mixed. A low prior for undocumented monumental casting is a prior, stated as such.

treatment.plainLanguage: The central claim: somewhere, at least one great stone monument contains stone that was made, not carved.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: This is the thesis itself; it stands or falls with the Egyptian (GEO-C020) and Andean (GEO-C021) instances.
treatment.strongestObjection: Every independent test of monument stone reads it as natural; the one positive comes from one team, on a fragment of undocumented origin (GEO-E057).
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent laboratory reproducing the interior organic matter in a documented Pumapunku andesite fragment, against natural Khapia andesite
An independent negative at Pumapunku, such as the features reproduced in natural Khapia andesite, which would move the verdict toward contradicted

claimAssessments.reasoning: Four independent petrographic records undermine it. GEO-E018 finds bedding, fossils and block-confined fractures across many blocks. GEO-E019 finds the showcase Lauer sample natural. GEO-E021 finds opal-CT, not synthetic cristobalite. GEO-E020's genuine geopolymer control shows an alkali binder is visible when present and absent from casing stone; GEO-E012's Si-rich spheres also occur in natural Tura stone. GEO-E017's calcium-silicate reading lies outside GEO-E020's test and is unrebutted, but no record has looked for that binder and found it. GEO-E033 removes the salt as support. The sample-identity dispute is recorded on GEO-E019 and GEO-E020.

treatment.plainLanguage: Some of the Great Pyramid's outer and backing blocks were cast, not quarried.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The only instance tested with methods that can see a binder. A positive would establish the thesis; the negative removes the most famous case.
treatment.strongestObjection: The negative tests targeted the alkali recipe. The lime–silica cement of GEO-E017 has never been looked for, and Davidovits disputes that the analysed Lauer piece was authentic.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Blinded NMR finding a calcium-silicate cement in securely sourced casing stone that a broad natural Tura, Dahshur and Giza suite lacks
A blinded paleomagnetic survey showing many blocks share a field-aligned direction absent from natural Mokattam limestone

claimAssessments.reasoning: Supported by GEO-E006 (sandstone, slab No. 2) and GEO-E007 (andesite organic matter): one team, one sample series. GEO-E057 shows the andesite was a loose surface find chosen by appearance; GEO-E060 that no natural andesite was compared. GEO-E036 restates earlier results and GEO-E062 offers unmeasured surface morphology; neither carries weight. The only negative, GEO-E008, is a 1971 sandstone provenance study that cannot exclude same-quarry aggregate. Positive records from one interested team with no independent negative make this weakly supported, not unresolved.

treatment.plainLanguage: Some andesite and red sandstone blocks at Pumapunku in Bolivia were cast.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The only instance where laboratory evidence on monument stone points toward casting; independent confirmation would settle the thesis.
treatment.strongestObjection: One team, a loose andesite fragment of undocumented origin, and no natural comparator. At Giza, similar microscope features proved to occur in natural stone.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent SEM and organic analysis of a catalogued andesite fragment against a Khapia control, with criteria fixed in advance
A radiocarbon date on the andesite organic matter: near AD 600 toward casting, modern toward contamination
A survey of Cerro Khapia finding quarry faces and dressing debris, or only natural sand

claimAssessments.reasoning: As a description of what the papers report, well supported: GEO-E006 and GEO-E007 state the findings, and GEO-E058 reports the interior occurrence. The same records limit what the reports show. GEO-E057 records a loose surface find, GEO-E060 no natural andesite compared, and GEO-E059 nitrogen only semi-quantitative, with residue or binder undecided. GEO-E061 shows amorphous pockets were seen in 1892, and GEO-E066 that the promised radiocarbon date has not been located. The report is credible; its weight for casting is not high.

treatment.plainLanguage: Two 2019 papers report organic matter and unusual microstructures in Pumapunku stone.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: True as a report, but non-independent, without a natural comparator and on stone of uncertain identity, so it moves the thesis only modestly.
treatment.strongestObjection: Volcanic rocks can host glassy and organic phases naturally; the criteria for calling them artificial were never blind-tested.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The same features reproduced in natural Khapia andesite
Independent reproduction in a documented monument fragment

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record is attached to this claim itself. The disclosed basis is GEO-E057, attached to the parent claim GEO-C004. It records the authors' own statement that PP1 was chosen by its flat surface from debris outside the protected monument area. The peer-reviewed version of that statement has not been read, so support is provisional. The admission runs against the authors' interest, which raises its credibility.

treatment.plainLanguage: The analysed andesite was picked up loose on the site, not cut from a known block.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Caps the weight of the andesite result: a loose fragment cannot show the monument was cast unless its origin is documented.
treatment.strongestObjection: Loose fragments with the characteristic flat face may well be pieces of the monument; lying outside the protected area does not prove otherwise.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Collection records, photographs or a refit tying the fragment to a catalogued block
The peer-reviewed paper stating a different sampling context

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record is attached to this claim itself. The disclosed basis is GEO-E058, attached to the parent claim GEO-C004, which reports the interior subsample PP1C and its spectrum. It is the same team and fragment as GEO-E007. EDS is elemental and cannot identify the organic compound. Provisional as a report of an observation.

treatment.plainLanguage: When cut open, the fragment is reported to hold the same organic-looking matter inside, beneath its crystals.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The strongest part of the andesite result: it makes surface dirt an incomplete explanation, but cannot tell a binder from natural or infiltrated matter.
treatment.strongestObjection: Without molecular identification or a natural control, an interior occurrence in one fragment says little about how the stone formed.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent molecular analysis of the interior matter
The same interior matter found in natural Khapia andesite

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E035 states the model directly in the proponents' 2020 abstract: natural uncrushed Khapia sand stored at Iwawe Stratum V, and the piedras cansadas never used. As a description of a theory it is well supported, though only the abstract was read. It is not evidence that the model is true.

treatment.plainLanguage: The proponents now say the andesite was cast from natural volcanic sand from Cerro Khapia, stored at Iwawe, and that the abandoned blocks were never used.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Describes rather than evidences, but makes the Andean branch testable at Iwawe and Khapia, where the two accounts predict different things.
treatment.strongestObjection: The model is stated at abstract level and presents no compositional test tying the Iwawe deposit to Khapia sand or to monument stone.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The Iwawe deposit shown to be dressing debris or airfall ash
Khapia surveyed and found to have, or lack, quarry faces

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E064 reports a laboratory replication of the acid-medium binder, but with modern chemicals and no data. It also states that plant acids cannot disaggregate andesite, and its second reader disputes the supporting direction. GEO-E059 records that the authors cannot tell guano residue from binder. No record shows the three-stage chemistry working with the proposed ancient inputs, so the verdict is unresolved rather than weakly supported.

treatment.plainLanguage: The proposed Andean recipe: plant acids, rock and seabird guano make durable stone without modern chemicals.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The mechanism the Andean account needs; showing it works would make that account possible, not show it happened.
treatment.strongestObjection: The only reported replication used modern reagents, and the authors concede acids do not attack andesite.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A published replication with plant extracts and guano, with the product analysed
A documented failure using the proposed inputs

claimAssessments.reasoning: The narrow point holds. GEO-E024 states that PXRF and ICP-MS cannot see H, C or O, which limits GEO-E009's Stonehenge match and any Khapia provenance argument. The claim overreaches in two places. It lists XRD as blind, although XRD reads crystalline binder phases, and GEO-E024's own table lists NMR as blind to Si. GEO-E020's positive control shows binder-aware petrography detects a binder when one is present. Correct in part and wrong in part: mixed.

treatment.plainLanguage: The chemistry used to match stones to quarries cannot tell carved stone from stone cast with sand from the same quarry.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Decides how far provenance studies constrain casting: fully for trace-element matching, not at all for direct microscopy.
treatment.strongestObjection: Cast stone needs a binder, and binders leave signatures that microscopy and diffraction do see (GEO-E020).
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A quarry-matched monument stone shown by binder-aware methods to contain a binder
A methods audit showing provenance studies already measured binder phases

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E022 shows lime and diatomaceous earth form a C–S–H cement at room temperature. GEO-E013 reports multi-ton demonstration blocks, self-reported and never independently analysed. GEO-E012 reports pyramid features read as reconstituted limestone, but their diagnosticity is disputed. The chemistry is shown to work; block-scale production with ancient inputs rests mainly on the proponents' own report, so the verdict is provisional.

treatment.plainLanguage: Artificial limestone that looks and behaves like the real thing can be made with ancient materials.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Necessary for casting, but showing it can be done says nothing about whether it was done.
treatment.strongestObjection: No demonstration block has been independently analysed, and modern know-how is not ancient practice.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent analysis of a demonstration block made with ancient inputs
A documented failure to reach natural-stone hardness with ancient materials

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E016 is a proponent's citation of Badari-period glassmaking as a temperature precedent, unverified here. The provisional grade leans on a prior, stated as such: ancient metallurgy routinely reached comparable temperatures with charcoal and bellows. Heat in a crucible is not industrial-scale processing.

treatment.plainLanguage: Ancient furnaces could reach the roughly 850 °C that natron chemistry needs.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A precondition for the natron route that the orthodox account can grant at no cost.
treatment.strongestObjection: Reaching a temperature in a crucible is not processing tons of material.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Evidence of large-scale natron-silicate processing installations
The Badari precedent shown to be misdated

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E010, a mainstream peer-reviewed study, identifies Wadi el Natrun and al-Barnuj as the primary natron sources and documents their 7th–9th century decline. GEO-E011 supplies the compositional typology behind such timelines. Uncontested.

treatment.plainLanguage: Egypt had large natron deposits, worked from antiquity and declining in the early Middle Ages.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Establishes an ingredient; the studies concern glass and faience and say nothing about stone.
treatment.strongestObjection: Natron available for glass is no evidence it was used for stone.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Evidence of natron in monument stone beyond what native salts explain

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E015 is an unattributed anecdote in a proponent book, and no controlled replication exists. It is weakly supported at most.

treatment.plainLanguage: Old fire pits can accidentally make stone from ash, suggesting how the craft was discovered.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: An origin story: its failure would not refute casting, and its success would not show it.
treatment.strongestObjection: The one report is unattributed and uncontrolled.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A controlled multi-month fire-pit trial producing stone-like material
Such a trial failing

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E001 reports the rate from a peer-reviewed photogrammetric study; GEO-E002 records Engelbach's report as the older basis. The study used a single team and tool configuration, so replication would help, but the measurement is sound as reported.

treatment.plainLanguage: A modern experiment measured how fast a dolerite pounder removes granite: about 216 cubic centimetres an hour.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Strains a pounding-only timeline, but fire-setting, chisels or more labour absorb the shortfall without casting.
treatment.strongestObjection: Skilled ancient crews with maintained tools may outperform an experimental protocol.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent replication with a substantially higher rate
Low rates replicated across techniques and granite types

claimAssessments.reasoning: This claim is held on its source statement only — Fóti's characterisation of Engelbach — with no evidence record extracted from the monograph; those extractions were blocked. GEO-E002, attached to GEO-C001 and GEO-C002, itself notes that the characterisation is unverified. It is graded unresolved under the rule for claims resting on a source statement alone.

treatment.plainLanguage: A proponent says the orthodox pounding account rests on one short hand-pounding trial by Engelbach in 1922.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Bears on the history of the orthodox account, not on casting.
treatment.strongestObjection: The characterisation comes from a book found to misstate three other sources.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Engelbach's text read and the characterisation confirmed or corrected

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E003 is Fóti's report of an unquantified visitor experience; GEO-E002 is context. No survey of attempts or of the block's wear exists. Weakly supported, as an anecdote.

treatment.plainLanguage: Visitors at Aswan have never managed to make a scoop mark with an ancient pounder.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Brief, untrained attempts say little about what organised crews could do.
treatment.strongestObjection: Tourists strike for moments; ancient crews worked for months.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A systematic trial on the test block recording effort against depth

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E005 is Fóti's description. The shafts' dimensions have not been independently surveyed, and the claim that a worker could not pound at the bottom is untested. Weakly supported.

treatment.plainLanguage: Deep shafts beside the obelisk trench seem too narrow to swing a pounder in.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Both readings, test pits and settling vessels, are unmeasured, so the shafts decide nothing yet.
treatment.strongestObjection: The conventional reading takes them for prospecting pits, which need not have been cut by full-swing pounding.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A survey of the shafts' geometry and floor residues

claimAssessments.reasoning: The only record, GEO-E045, undermines it. The dolerite comes from dykes within the Aswan granite, with Pharaonic tool-production quarries and pounder-sized blanks near the obelisk. No record supports a non-pounding purpose. Confidence is low because the survey does not test what the pounders struck, describes their wear only qualitatively, and notes that Engelbach judged the stone non-local.

treatment.plainLanguage: The Aswan pounding stones were brought in to grind or tamp a casting mix, not to pound granite.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Central to the natron route's reading of the quarry; weak for the thesis as a whole.
treatment.strongestObjection: Nobody has analysed the pounders' wear to see what material they struck.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Microwear showing glass-abrasion wear on the pounders
Microwear showing granite-percussion wear, which would close the question

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E027 finds that al-Suyūṭī's two detailed entries on the breach mention no salt. GEO-E029 shows the report's only carrier is a proponent page citing no medieval source, and GEO-E028 shows its 820 date matches nothing shown. GEO-E004 is that same uncited report. Contradicted, with low confidence, because other medieval authors remain unread.

treatment.plainLanguage: Medieval accounts of the Caliph's break-in report salt-coated chamber walls.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Even if sourced, the salt would not discriminate, since halite is reported native to Giza limestone.
treatment.strongestObjection: Absence from one compilation does not prove that no Arabic author reports it.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A located medieval Arabic passage reporting the salt

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E030 confirms the salt is halite but makes no comparison. GEO-E031 records halite efflorescence at other Egyptian limestone sites, including the carved-bedrock Sphinx. GEO-E032 reports halite as native to Giza limestone, second-hand. GEO-E026 is an uncontrolled taste test against the wrong comparator. The comparative premise fails.

treatment.plainLanguage: The pyramid's stones carry salt that comparable natural limestone does not.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Both accounts predict salt in the blocks, so it cannot choose between them.
treatment.strongestObjection: No salt concentrations have been compared between pyramid stone and unworked bedrock.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Unworked Giza and Mokattam bedrock found free of halite efflorescence
Bulk chloride in pyramid blocks that bedrock lacks

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E030 reports XRD of seven samples and SEM-EDX finding only halite, calcite and quartz, in a peer-reviewed study using modern instruments. Only efflorescence and detached fragments were sampled.

treatment.plainLanguage: The white crust inside the pyramid is common salt, with calcite and quartz and nothing else.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Confirms the salt but says nothing about its origin.
treatment.strongestObjection: Surface sampling cannot say whether the salt runs through the blocks.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Cored samples showing different phases

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E032 reports Na and Cl in material from unaffected areas, which the authors read as inherent to the stone. It also cites Klemm & Klemm for halite as a primary sedimentary constituent. That book has not been read and no stone was cored, so support is provisional. The second reader's dissent, that the record supports rather than undermines this claim, is how it is weighed here.

treatment.plainLanguage: Salt is naturally part of the plateau's limestone, laid down from evaporating seawater.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If confirmed, it removes salt as a sign of casting.
treatment.strongestObjection: The key statement is a second-hand citation, and no bedrock comparison has been measured.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Klemm & Klemm read directly
XRD of efflorescence on unworked bedrock and Tura quarry faces

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E034 documents undocumented 1995–97 cleaning and filling inside the Khufu pyramid, a sulfur-rich modern fill, and salt re-forming within two years. The general claim about megalithic sites is unaudited; one strong instance supports it provisionally.

treatment.plainLanguage: Few monuments have a full restoration record, so odd surface features may be modern.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Cuts both ways: it weakens surface arguments for casting and surface observations against it.
treatment.strongestObjection: One instance does not show the pattern holds at every site.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An audit of restoration histories at the disputed sites

claimAssessments.reasoning: GEO-E014 is Fóti's interpretive reading. Egyptology reads the scene as metal casting and has not engaged the reinterpretation. Weakly supported, as an argument that has been made.

treatment.plainLanguage: A tomb painting usually read as metal casting may instead show mineral processing.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A picture cannot show what was in the crucibles.
treatment.strongestObjection: The conventional metal-casting reading is standard, and the reinterpretation comes from a proponent alone.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A re-examination identifying the residues or tools each reading predicts, and finding them
